title: The alphabet

objectives.can: Name each of the twenty-four lower-case letters and give its sound.

explanation.summary: Greek is written in an alphabet of twenty-four letters. Every word you will read in this course is made of them, so the first job is to know each letter by sight, by name and by sound.

sections.heading: Twenty-four letters
body: The first table of this lesson lists the lower-case letters in their alphabetical order, with the name each letter has in English, the usual way of writing it in Latin letters (its transliteration), and the sound it is given in the school convention that most beginners' courses use. That convention is a teaching device: lesson G0.3.1 sets it beside the other ways Greek is pronounced, and the choice never changes how a word is spelled.
Seven of the letters are vowels: α ε η ι ο υ ω. The other seventeen are consonants. Two of the consonants, ξ and ψ, each stand for two sounds written as one letter (ks and ps).

Learn the letters themselves, not their transliterations. A Greek text never prints transliteration, so the aim is to look at λόγος and see five letters at once, not to translate it into English letters first.

sections.heading: Letters that look like other letters
body: Many Greek letters resemble Latin letters and stand for something else. Reading ρ as p, ν as v or η as n is the commonest beginner's error. The second table of this lesson lists the main traps. Look at each one slowly in a real word: in ἄνθρωπος the letter after θ is rho and the one before the final omicron is pi.
Two letters also differ in length from their look-alikes: ε and ο are short vowels, while η and ω are their long partners. The next lessons say more about long and short vowels.

sections.heading: Two letters that make one sound
body: Gamma is a hard g, as in 'go'. When it stands before another gamma or before κ, ξ or χ it is read as the n of 'finger': ἄγγελος is read 'angelos'. The same combination does not change how the word is spelled.

sections.heading: What the letters do not show
body: Printed Greek puts small marks over and under the letters, and it has capital letters and a second shape of sigma. None of these are needed yet. Lesson G0.1.2 teaches the capitals and the second sigma; lessons G0.2.1 and G0.2.2 teach the vowel marks, breathings and accents. For now read past them and attend to the letters.

misunderstandings: ν is not v, ρ is not p, η is not n, ω is not w, χ is not x and υ is not a plain u. Each of these looks like a Latin letter and is a different Greek letter with a different sound.
Transliteration is a help for talking about a word, not a spelling to learn. Greek words are always learned in Greek letters.
The sounds in the table are a teaching convention, not a recording of how first-century speakers talked. Lesson G0.3.1 shows the other traditions.

deeper.heading: Where the letters came from
body: The Greeks took their alphabet from a Semitic one used in Phoenicia. The names alpha and beta are from the same source as the Hebrew letter names aleph and beth. The Greeks used some signs that had stood for consonants not found in Greek to write vowels, which is why Greek is written with full vowel letters.

paradigms.title: Letters easily mistaken for Latin letters
paradigms.caption: look-alikes
head: Greek letter
Name
Looks like
What to remember
rows: It is the Greek n. It only looks like v.
It is a vowel written y in transliteration, and it is the second half of αυ, ευ and ου.
It is r. The Greek letter for p is π.
It is a long e. The Greek letter for n is ν.
It is a long o. The short o is ο.
It is ch, as in 'loch'. The letter for ks is ξ.
It is g. It never sounds like y in this convention.

examples.analysis: λόγος is five letters: lambda, omicron, gamma, omicron, sigma (the sigma at the end has its special shape, taught in the next lesson). In the school convention it is read 'LO-gos'. θεόν is theta, epsilon, omicron, nu: the last letter looks like v but is nu, an n. The word is read 'the-ON'.

examples.analysis: ζωή is zeta, omega, eta. Both vowels are the long ones, so a transliteration marks them ō and ē: zōē. φῶς is phi, omega, sigma: phi has no English look-alike and is read 'ph' as in 'phone'; omega is the long o. Compare ο (omicron), the short o, which stands in λόγος.

examples.analysis: ἄνθρωπος has two letters that deceive English readers side by side: rho (ρ, r) and pi (π, p). The word begins alpha, nu, theta, rho, omega, pi, omicron, sigma. ὄνομα has two omicrons, the short o, and ends in alpha.

check.prompt: How many letters does the Greek alphabet have, and how many of them are vowels?
check.explain: There are twenty-four letters. The vowels are α ε η ι ο υ ω, seven in all. English has five vowel letters, but Greek writes the long e and long o with their own letters, η and ω.

reading.why: Five verses of plain words, a name (Ἰωάννης), and several of the look-alike letters (ν, ρ, π, υ, ω), so that you can practise naming letters in a continuous text. Do not try to translate; read the letters aloud one by one.
